newsitem.title: UK: Hague leads race for UK Conservative leadership.
newsitem.headline: Hague leads race for UK Conservative leadership.

text.p: William Hague, front-runner in the race to take over the leadership of Britain's Conservative party, won backing from a key ally of Margaret Thatcher on Tuesday, boosting his chances of succeeding former prime minister John Major.

A week before the first round of the election for the leader of Britain's opposition, former cabinet minister Lord Parkinson said Hague, just 36, represented "a new generation for the new century ... a fresh start".

"It is time for the Conservative Party to choose a leader from a new generation for the new century. I believe that leader should be William Hague," said Parkinson, a former Conservative party chairman.

Bookmakers said punters were also putting their money on Hague. Corals said business was "brisk" with Hague favourite at 5/4, followed by the former chancellor of the exchequer (finance minister), Kenneth Clarke, in a field of six candidates.

Hague, who became the youngest cabinet member in nearly 50 years when Major made him Welsh Secretary in 1995, failed to win the endorsement of Major, who is stepping aside to allow his party to regroup after Labour's crushing election victory on May 1.

In his first full radio interview since the defeat, Major told the BBC: "I will vote, I will make my own choice in the secrecy of the ballot. I have no intention of indicating to anybody else for whom I will vote."
Major's refusal to back Hague was in contrast to his own election to head the Conservatives in November 1990. Then, ousted prime minister Thatcher gave Major her blessing.
Hague's appeal lies in a combination of right-wing views and youth. He first hit the headlines as a 16-year-old when he made a rousing speech to the Conservative Party conference.

Hague is still trading on his image as a boy wonder and is also playing on his northern English roots -- a plus in a party with just 165 members in the 659-seat parliament and thinly represented outside London.

Hague has admitted the need to learn the lessons from Labour's slick election campaign, but critics say that despite his youth, Hague is short of new ideas to lift morale in his dispirited party, in power for 18 years before May 1.

A poor start to his campaign, when he apparently toasted a deal to back the leadership campaign of former interior minister Michael Howard with champagne only to back out in the morning, has also raised questions about his judgment.
